title: The Devil Wears Prada 2
synopsis: Print is dead. Miranda Priestly is not. She has summoned you back to Runway — fifteen years older, a real career later, and with a daughter you can't be late to pick up. The September issue is a relaunch. Try not to fall apart.

nodes.text: The email comes from an assistant whose name you don't know. 'Miranda would like to see you Tuesday.' No subject line. No greeting. No indication of which Tuesday, or what Tuesday means, or whether declining is a category of behavior that exists. You read it three times in your kitchen, holding a lunchbox with a dinosaur on it.

choices.text: Reply immediately to confirm
choices.consequence: You reply in four minutes, one line, ending in a period and no exclamation point. Fifteen years off and your thumbs still know the drill.

choices.text: Wait a day; you have a life now
choices.consequence: You leave it sitting for twenty-two hours, which feels enormous to you and registers at Runway as absolutely nothing at all.

nodes.text: The lobby smells the same — cold stone, lilies, somebody's third espresso. Your heart, humiliatingly, knows which elevator button before your hand does. Miranda's office is unchanged except that the wall of stacked magazines is gone, and in its place stands one iPad on one stand, lit from below, like something in a chapel.

choices.text: Compliment the iPad
choices.consequence: You say something admiring about the screen. Miranda looks at you the way you'd look at a man complimenting the weather during a robbery.

choices.text: Wait until she speaks
choices.consequence: You stand there in silence for forty seconds. You win. Nobody outlasts Miranda Priestly, but today, on one narrow technicality, you do.

nodes.text: Wednesday, school drop-off, second in the car line. Beatrix is unbuckling and eating a granola bar and asks, with no particular weight, whether you're going back to 'the shouty job.' You have never once called it that in front of her. She waves, gets out, and leaves you holding a wrapper and a small crisis.

choices.text: Tell her about the meeting
choices.consequence: You tell her the truth through the passenger window while the car behind you leans on the horn. She says 'cool' and is gone.

choices.text: Tell her it's just lunch
choices.consequence: You tell her it's only lunch. She accepts this instantly, which is somehow worse than if she had pushed back on it.

nodes.text: Editor at Large. A quarterly print object that is also, per the deck, 'a digital ecosystem.' A hundred dollars a copy. The salary is real in a way that makes you sit back an inch, and Miranda notices the inch. She does not mention hours. She does not mention weekends. She mentions the paper stock, at length.

choices.text: Negotiate for hours that fit your life
choices.consequence: You say the words 'I leave at five on Tuesdays and Thursdays' out loud in that office. The ceiling declines to collapse.

choices.text: Take the job and figure it out
choices.consequence: You say yes before she has finished describing the cover stock. Fifteen years of hard-won perspective, undone by a font.

nodes.text: An old colleague calls from a serious magazine with a serious offer: steady, respected, half the money, and an editor who says thank you in complete sentences. Both offers land in the same week, because that is how weeks work. You write the two salaries on the back of a school permission slip and then stare at the permission slip.

choices.text: Take the steadier job
choices.consequence: You take the quiet one, and for roughly six hours you feel like a grown adult, and then you feel something else entirely.

choices.text: Take Miranda's job; you can survive her now
choices.consequence: You take the loud one. You are forty-one, you have survived worse things than her, and the honest truth is you missed it.

nodes.text: Emily Charlton arrives as a consultant now, running partnerships for a house whose name people pronounce slowly. Two phones, no notebook. She spots you across the floor and for one unguarded second she smiles — then corrects it into something more expensive and sits down. Neither of you mentions Paris. Neither of you ever will.

choices.text: Approach Emily like an old friend
choices.consequence: You hug her. She endures it like a customs search, and then at the door asks about your daughter, by name, correctly.

choices.text: Approach Emily as a future colleague
choices.consequence: You shake her hand and open with margins. She visibly relaxes. Emily has always preferred a spreadsheet to a feeling.

nodes.text: 'Did you have a fun day at work?' Beatrix is ten and asks it the way she has been taught to ask it, at a school where adults apparently have fun at work. You open your mouth. Nothing arrives. The pause runs long enough that she stops chewing and looks up, genuinely curious now.

choices.text: Tell her some days are fun and some aren't
choices.consequence: You give her the true version, with the boring parts left in. She nods slowly, files it, and asks whether that's also true about school.

choices.text: Tell her you'll have more fun days now
choices.consequence: You promise her more fun days. She believes you completely, which means you are now contractually obligated to arrange some.

nodes.text: The plan is ambitious, expensive, and statistically doomed: a quarterly object that costs a hundred dollars and sells out anyway. Miranda wants the lead feature to read as a manifesto and photograph as a fashion story, at once, with no visible seam. She says this in a single sentence, then waits, as if she has described something reasonable.

choices.text: Pitch a story about the daughters of fashion editors
choices.consequence: You pitch the daughters of fashion editors. Miranda goes still for three seconds — the good still — and says 'possibly,' which is a standing ovation.

choices.text: Pitch a story about climate-positive supply chains
choices.consequence: You pitch supply chains at a magazine that sells handbags. Emily's eyebrows go up. Miranda's do not, which is the entire answer.

nodes.text: Your husband spreads the calendar across the table like a man defusing something. Pickups, his deadlines, the Tuesday swim thing, the six weeks each spring when fashion eats the world. The math is tight. The math is, with two adjustments and one paid sitter, genuinely possible. He circles April and says nothing about April.

choices.text: Adjust the math together
choices.consequence: You move two of his deadlines and one of your dinners and it works perfectly on paper. Paper has never been the problem.

choices.text: Take a month to test the new schedule before committing
choices.consequence: You run a trial month. It breaks in week three, in a pediatrician's waiting room, and now you know exactly which part breaks.

nodes.text: You hire a photographer Miranda has publicly disliked since 2011. He is brilliant and slow and the shoot runs four hours past the call sheet. She walks onto set in the last hour, studies the monitor, says nothing for thirty seconds, then: 'Continue.' Everyone exhales. In her language, that was a parade with horses.

choices.text: Send the photographer a handwritten note
choices.consequence: You write him four lines on Runway letterhead. He photographs the note and posts it. Miranda sees the post and says nothing, twice.

choices.text: Move on to the next shoot with confidence
choices.consequence: You book the next three shoots by dinner. Confidence is mostly calendar entries made before the fear has time to catch up.

nodes.text: The supply-chain piece will be the first thing several of your old fashion friends actually read rather than merely hold. It will also annoy two advertisers, one of whom buys a full page every issue and sends a Christmas hamper the size of a toddler. You consider the hamper problem for a while and decide you can live without it.

choices.text: Run it on the cover
choices.consequence: You put it on the cover. The advertiser calls, furious. Miranda takes the call, says nine words, and the advertiser renews.

choices.text: Run it as the lead of the inside well
choices.consequence: You run it two spreads back, where it goes unbothered and gets read anyway. Cowardice and strategy share a great deal of DNA.

nodes.text: School holiday, so Beatrix comes in. Miranda meets her by the elevators. They shake hands with matching gravity. Miranda compliments the shoes — out loud, sincerely, in front of witnesses. Then Beatrix looks around a floor holding a hundred working adults and asks, with total calm, what the office is actually for.

choices.text: Let Miranda answer
choices.consequence: Miranda answers in one sentence about beauty being a form of argument. Beatrix says 'okay' and asks where the snacks live.

choices.text: Answer for both of you
choices.consequence: You answer it yourself. It takes ninety seconds and it is the clearest you have ever been about your own job. Miranda listens to all of it.

nodes.text: Nigel starts a thread with you and Emily and gives it a name you would not read aloud. It becomes the place the worst forty minutes of any given day goes to die. Emily sends screenshots with no comment. Nigel sends voice notes from a corner office two time zones away. Nobody explains context, because nobody needs it.

choices.text: Use the chat as a daily lifeline
choices.consequence: You post everything, daily, at volume, and they absorb all of it. Nigel starts replying with one emoji that means 'I know.'

choices.text: Use it sparingly; don't drain it
choices.consequence: You ration yourself to twice a week. Emily notices the rationing and texts you privately, which is as close as Emily gets to a hug.

nodes.text: The relaunch sells out in twelve days. Three newspapers that have never covered fashion pick up the supply-chain feature. Resale copies go for triple online, a fact Miranda pretends not to know and mentions twice in one meeting. On her way to the elevator she smiles at you. Once. Briefly. It counts, and you will take it.

choices.text: Stay on for the next issue
choices.consequence: You commit to one more issue. 'One more issue' is what people say roughly six years before they finally leave.

choices.text: Make a longer-term commitment
choices.consequence: You sign three years with the Tuesday-and-Thursday clause written into the contract. Legal calls it 'unusual.' It stays in anyway.

nodes.text: You leave the launch before the speeches, which nobody notices, because nobody at a launch has ever noticed anything. At home the two of them are still up and there is pizza going cold on the coffee table. You sit on the floor in the dress and eat two slices with your shoes off. Best half hour of the month.

choices.text: Make this the routine — leave early on purpose
choices.consequence: You start ducking out before the speeches at every event. Your reputation takes zero damage. Nobody was listening to the speeches.

choices.text: Take Beatrix to the next launch
choices.consequence: You bring her to the next one. She eats nine canapés, corners a designer about fabric dye, and critiques the lighting on the ride home.

nodes.text: Year two is harder, because year two always is. The novelty burns off, two advertisers leave and come back, and the print run has to be defended in a room full of people who say the word 'attention' as a noun. You and Emily and Nigel have become, without ever discussing it, a cabinet. Miranda never acknowledges this. She also never fires any of you.

choices.text: Take the editor-in-chief role when offered
choices.consequence: You start behaving like the person who runs the place months before anybody offers it to you. Nobody stops you. Nobody ever does.

choices.text: Stay as Editor at Large and write more
choices.consequence: You decline the bigger title and file four thousand words instead. Emily calls you an idiot, affectionately, in writing, twice.

nodes.text: Beatrix, twelve, announces she wants to write. Not fashion — science, and specifically things that live in cold water. She has a list of magazines and has already emailed two of them without mentioning it to you. You arrange an internship at one, then have to sit quietly with the fact that she'd have landed it herself.

choices.text: Mentor a new generation through her
choices.consequence: You start taking her friends' emails seriously. Six of them over four years. Two end up with bylines you had nothing to do with.

choices.text: Stay focused on your own work
choices.consequence: You let her run her own campaign and go back to yours. She never needed the ladder. She needed one phone number and got it.

nodes.text: Miranda announces it over lunch for eight at a restaurant with no sign on the door. She says the word 'retiring' the way other people say 'Tuesday.' Then she looks directly at you while saying the next part. Emily looks at you. Nigel looks, with enormous concentration, at a salad that has nothing on it.

choices.text: Volunteer for the role
choices.consequence: You say 'I'd like it' in a level voice at a table of eight. Miranda cuts a piece of fish and does not look up from the fish.

choices.text: Volunteer Emily
choices.consequence: You put Emily's name forward instead. She kicks you under the table hard enough to bruise, then takes the meeting on Monday.

nodes.text: You drop her at a building with a whale skeleton hanging in the lobby. She is less nervous than you are by an embarrassing margin. The editor shakes her hand, then yours, and says 'we've heard,' which could mean six different things. Walking back to the subway you understand that you did not raise a child. You raised a person.

choices.text: Take the afternoon off to mark it
choices.consequence: You take the afternoon, sit in a park, and answer nothing. Runway survives four unsupervised hours, which is useful information.

choices.text: Go back to work changed
choices.consequence: You go straight in and rewrite the whole cover line on the train. It's better. She did that, indirectly, from a lobby.

nodes.text: September again. Nine cover options are laid across your desk and the decision belongs to you now, which is new. You stand over them holding cold coffee, and somewhere around the third version you understand that this is not a cover decision at all. It is a decision about who you intend to be until you're sixty.

choices.text: Take the EIC role and build the next decade
choices.consequence: You choose the loud cover and the big chair. Ten minutes later somebody asks you to approve a font, and it has begun.

choices.text: Stay Editor at Large and write the better book
choices.consequence: You choose the quiet cover and keep the title that lets you leave at five. Emily calls it a waste. Emily is wrong, mostly.

nodes.text: You take the chair. The first thing you change is the meeting culture, the second is what the interns get paid, and neither makes the trade press. Miranda, from a house in the south of France she claims to hate, sends one card in that handwriting: 'Don't be me. Be better.' You frame it and hang it where you'll see it during arguments. Some days you manage it. On the other days you know the note is there.

You keep the title that lets you write and still make the pool by five-forty. In your fifties you publish a collection about clothes and the people who actually make them, and it wins a small prize nobody in fashion has heard of and every editor privately wants. Beatrix sits in the front row in a borrowed blazer, filing copy on her phone for a magazine about cold water, and doesn't clap until the very end.
